definition: Slow to act, or tending to put things off and cause delay.
example: The dilatory landlord took six weeks to fix a leaking faucet.
nuance: Tardy just means late, but dilatory suggests a habit or tactic of stalling. It has nothing to do with dilated, which means widened.
prompt: A town committee has postponed its vote on the library budget for the third time.
options: The committee's dilatory approach left the library unable to order new books.
The dilatory committee approved the budget within minutes of hearing the proposal.
The doctor checked whether the patient's pupils were dilatory after the eye drops.
The dilatory members dabbled in budgeting as a hobby without any real expertise.
reasons: Putting off a decision again and again is exactly the stalling this word describes.
Acting within minutes is prompt, the reverse of dragging one's feet.
Pupils that widen are dilated; the look-alike word concerns delay, not expansion.
Dabbling as an amateur describes a dilettante, not someone who keeps postponing.

practice.prompt: A student has a science report due on Friday morning.
options: Her dilatory habits had the report finished and proofread a week early.
She made the report more dilatory by stretching it from four pages to seven.
Staying up all night had a dilatory effect on her ability to focus in class.
Her dilatory habits meant the report sat untouched until Thursday night.
reasons: Finishing far ahead of the deadline is the opposite of procrastinating.
Making something longer is expanding it; the word refers to stalling, not length.
A harmful effect is deleterious; this look-alike describes delay, not damage.
Leaving the work until the last possible moment shows a habit of putting things off.
